title: Grant me this
hookLine: deh sivaa bar mohi ihai: grant that I never turn from good deeds and fear no foe (Dasam, Chandi Charitar)
last: HOLDING THE HEM · IN HIS REFUGE · MANY NAMES · THE LIGHT PASSES ON · YOU MADE ME WORTHY · TELL THE FRIEND.

lines: THIS ONE ASKS FOR A SPINE.
A VERSE CHILDREN LEARN TO SING.
cards: When people ask for something big, it's often comfort: let the test go well, let the scan be clear, let the money come through. Fair enough.
This verse asks for something else: the strength not to quit doing what's right, even when it costs. Not to be spared trouble, but to stay good inside it.
Sikhs hold it as the Tenth Guru's, and Sikh children learn to sing it.

teach.b: The verse comes near the end of Chandi Charitar, a long poem in the Dasam Granth. Its first words: deh sivaa bar mohi ihai.
In paraphrase: grant me this boon, that I never turn away from good deeds. That when I go to face the enemy, I'm not afraid, and I win with resolve.
That I teach my own mind this lesson: to sing Your praises. And when my life's end comes, let me die fighting in the field. Start with the first ask: subh karman te kabhoon na taro.
Never turn back from good deeds. That's the center of it. Courage in battle comes after it, and can be read as serving it.
Then notice who's being taught: my own mind. The verse doesn't ask God to change other people. It asks for a mind that keeps choosing good.
Who is Sivaa, the one being asked? Sikhs read it in different ways. Some hear Sivaa as a name for God's own power, the Timeless One, addressed by many names in the Dasam Granth.

Others read it within the setting of the poem, which tells of the goddess Chandi's battles, and hear the verse as the poet's request at its close. Scholars discuss it, and the verse is loved either way.
What stays is the shape of the request: a prayer for character, not circumstances.
The Khalsa ideal of the saint-soldier lives in those four lines: gentle enough to sing God's praise, steady enough never to walk away from what's right.

how: Sikhs sing deh sivaa bar mohi ihai at gatherings, in schools and in kirtan, often standing, as a prayer for steadiness in doing good.

o: good deeds, the ones never to turn from
lucky outcomes, granted as a boon
brave deeds done only in battle

games.q: grant me this — tap the pairs.

s: the verse mainly asks for an easy life
it asks never to turn from good deeds: character, not circumstances.
Sikhs read Sivaa in more than one way
some hear God's own power; others read it within the poem's story of Chandi.

games.q: you're writing a one-line request to God. what does the Tenth Guru's verse ask for first?
o: never to turn back from good deeds.
games.why: subh karman te kabhoon na taro: never turn from good deeds comes first; courage serves it.

practice: Sit up straight and think of one good thing you've been meaning to do and keep putting off: a visit, an apology, a donation, standing up for someone. Picture the moment you'd want to back out, and picture yourself not backing out.
If you pray, say the verse's first words, deh sivaa bar mohi ihai, or Waheguru.

wordCard.voice: Subh karman, good deeds: the Tenth Guru's verse asks, in paraphrase, that I never turn from them, never fear when I face the enemy, and teach my own mind to sing Your praise.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: good deeds; the verse asks never to turn from them.

carryVoice: Your line: never turn from good. Not an easy road, but a steady spine. Day six hundred seventy-two, done.

sources.ref: Chandi Charitar (Ukti Bilas), savaiya near the close (deh sivaa bar mohi ihai)
